title: Starting Anchor
question: What should a forecaster establish before considering the specific details of a case?
correctExplanation: Right. The general frequency of similar cases is the sensible starting point for any estimate.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is base rates. Without a general figure, vivid details can pull an estimate far from reality.
lessonContent:
Start from the general, then adjust.
Frequencies anchor estimates.
Specifics refine, not replace, the baseline.
Begin with the background rate.
Share this: find the background frequency before judging one case.

title: From the Group
question: What is the name for estimating by comparing with similar completed cases rather than your own plan?
correctExplanation: Right. Looking at comparable cases corrects the optimism built into an inside plan.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the outside view. Judging from the group's experience counters the specialness we feel about our own case.
lessonContent:
Your plan feels unique; the data say otherwise.
Compare with the group, not just the sketch.
Adopt the observer's stance.
Use history as the corrective.
Share this: estimate one task from similar past cases.

title: Confidence Match
question: What quality describes a forecaster whose stated confidence matches their actual accuracy?
correctExplanation: Right. When ninety-percent claims come true ninety percent of the time, confidence is trustworthy.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is calibration. It is measured by comparing stated confidence with observed hit rates over many predictions.
lessonContent:
Confidence should match accuracy.
Measure hits across many forecasts.
Adjust confidence from the score.
Trust follows from calibration.
Share this: rate your confidence in one prediction, then check it later.

title: Better Than a Point
question: What should replace a single-number forecast to express uncertainty honestly?
correctExplanation: Right. A range communicates the real uncertainty that a lone figure hides.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a confidence range. It shows both a middle estimate and how far off it might be.
lessonContent:
Point estimates hide uncertainty.
Ranges communicate what is unknown.
Widen the range when evidence is thin.
State intervals with your forecast.
Share this: give one estimate as a range rather than a number.

title: Learning From Errors
question: What habit converts experience into improved judgement over time?
correctExplanation: Right. Recording predictions and outcomes shows where confidence drifts from reality.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is tracking your record. Regular feedback is how judgement learns its own biases.
lessonContent:
Unmeasured judgement cannot improve.
Feedback converts confidence into data.
Keep a record of forecasts and results.
Adjust your confidence from the score.
Share this: log one prediction today and set a date to check it.

title: Revising Belief
question: What should happen to a forecast when new relevant information arrives?
correctExplanation: Right. Beliefs should shift in proportion to how much the new information actually changes the odds.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is updating on evidence. Refusing to revise, or overreacting, both misread what new data warrant.
lessonContent:
Estimates should move with evidence.
Revise in proportion to relevance.
Avoid both stubbornness and overreaction.
Treat beliefs as adjustable.
Share this: revise one opinion based on a new fact today.

title: Breaking It Down
question: What technique improves difficult estimates by splitting the problem into smaller parts?
correctExplanation: Right. Estimating each component separately is easier and more accurate than guessing the whole at once.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is decomposition. Smaller pieces can be estimated with more confidence and then recombined.
lessonContent:
Large questions hide smaller ones.
Estimate parts, then recombine.
Smaller pieces are easier to judge.
Structure reduces uncertainty.
Share this: break one daunting estimate into three parts.

title: Group Benchmark
question: What is the formal name for forecasting a case from the distribution of similar past cases?
correctExplanation: Right. It anchors a projection in the outcomes of a comparable group rather than the specifics of a plan.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reference class forecasting. The group's outcomes set the baseline, then adjustments follow.
lessonContent:
Groups reveal what single cases cannot.
Baselines come from comparable outcomes.
Choose the class carefully.
Adjust from the baseline with evidence.
Share this: build a small comparison group for one decision.

title: Several Futures
question: What is the practice of planning for multiple distinct possible futures instead of one prediction?
correctExplanation: Right. Robustness across scenarios matters more than being right about one forecast.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is scenario planning. It exposes which choices survive regardless of which future arrives.
lessonContent:
Prediction is fragile; preparation is robust.
Consider a few divergent futures.
Look for choices that win in most of them.
Hedge what cannot be decided now.
Share this: sketch two futures that would change one plan of yours.

title: Before Launch
question: What exercise imagines a project has already failed so that risks can be listed in advance?
correctExplanation: Right. Assuming the failure has happened frees people to name worries they would otherwise withhold.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a premortem. It does not predict doom but enlarges the list of things worth watching.
lessonContent:
Dissent is easier when failure is assumed.
Naming risks lowers their surprise value.
Convert silence into a checklist.
Practise the failure before living it.
Share this: run a five-minute risk listing before your next big step.

title: Return to Normal
question: What statistical effect explains why an extreme result tends to be followed by a more ordinary one?
correctExplanation: Right. Extremes usually contain luck that does not repeat, so the next result drifts back.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is regression to the mean. Reading the return as failure, or the peak as a new normal, misreads random noise.
lessonContent:
Extremes contain luck as well as signal.
Expect drift after unusual results.
Judge changes against that drift.
Do not treat noise as a trend.
Share this: predict the likely drift after one extreme result.

title: Error and Scatter
question: What distinction separates a systematic shared error from random scatter between judges?
correctExplanation: Right. Bias is a consistent direction of error, while noise is unwanted variability around the target.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is noise versus bias. Both harm accuracy, but their causes and remedies differ.
lessonContent:
Error comes in two flavours.
Consistent skew is not the same as scatter.
Diagnose the type before correcting.
Reduce both for better judgement.
Share this: ask whether one error is directional or random.

title: Too Sure
question: What is the error of stating more certainty than the evidence supports?
correctExplanation: Right. Overconfidence shows up as narrow ranges and strong claims that facts do not justify.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is overconfidence. It is corrected by widening ranges and tracking how often confident claims hold.
lessonContent:
Confidence should track evidence.
Narrow ranges often overstate knowledge.
Measure hits to detect the gap.
Widen where evidence is thin.
Share this: widen one overconfident estimate today.

title: First Number Pull
question: What effect describes how an initial figure pulls later estimates toward it?
correctExplanation: Right. Even an arbitrary number becomes a reference that adjustments stay tied to.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is anchoring. The defence is to set your own estimate before hearing anyone else's figure.
lessonContent:
Initial values bias later judgement.
Even irrelevant numbers leave a trace.
Set your own reference first.
Adjust from evidence, not the opening.
Share this: decide your number before hearing another's.

title: Easy to Recall
question: What mental shortcut judges probability by how easily examples come to mind?
correctExplanation: Right. Vivid or recent cases feel more common than they are, distorting the judged frequency.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the availability heuristic. Headlines and memories, not base rates, end up setting the estimate.
lessonContent:
Ease of recall is not frequency.
Vivid cases inflate perceived risk.
Return to base rates when emotions spike.
Notice what memory is doing to your maths.
Share this: check a real frequency against a vivid recent event.

title: Once We Know
question: What bias makes outcomes seem obvious only after they have happened?
correctExplanation: Right. Once the answer is known, memory rewrites the past so the result feels predictable.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is hindsight bias. The cure is to record predictions beforehand and score them afterward.
lessonContent:
Memory is edited by what we now know.
Hindsight conceals genuine uncertainty.
Record forecasts before the fact.
Score them to calibrate judgement.
Share this: write one prediction before you learn the outcome.

title: Rough by Design
question: What estimation technique deliberately uses rounded figures to get a quick order of magnitude?
correctExplanation: Right. Comfortable round numbers are multiplied to reach a figure accurate enough for the decision.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Fermi estimation. Precision is sacrificed on purpose in exchange for speed and insight.
lessonContent:
Rough numbers can still inform decisions.
Round aggressively to keep the maths light.
Chain estimates across scales.
State assumptions with the result.
Share this: estimate one unknown quantity with round numbers.

title: Updating by Chances
question: What kind of reasoning combines a prior belief with the likelihood of new evidence?
correctExplanation: Right. It weighs how much more likely the evidence is under one hypothesis than another.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Bayes reasoning. It prevents both ignoring new data and overreacting to weak signals.
lessonContent:
Combine prior belief with new data.
Compare how likely evidence is under each view.
Update in proportion, not in leaps.
Avoid both rigidity and panic.
Share this: revise one belief after weighing new evidence.

title: Experts Who Score
question: What term describes forecasters who consistently outperform by updating carefully and keeping score?
correctExplanation: Right. Ordinary people who reason carefully and revise often can beat confident specialists.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is superforecasting. The edge comes from process, not from status or intuition.
lessonContent:
Method can beat reputation.
Careful updating and scoring help most.
Small edges compound over many predictions.
Focus on process.
Share this: adopt one forecasting habit for a week.

title: Always Late
question: What is the tendency to underestimate how long and how much a task will take called?
correctExplanation: Right. People forecast best-case scenarios and ignore how similar efforts actually went.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the planning fallacy. Comparing with past comparable work is the standard remedy.
lessonContent:
Plans skew optimistic.
Best cases crowd out the base rate.
Compare with how similar tasks ended.
Build buffers from history.
Share this: check one estimate against a past comparable task.

title: Ignoring the Odds
question: What error describes making a decision while disregarding the background frequency of an event?
correctExplanation: Right. Vivid specifics take over and the general frequency is dropped from the calculation.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the base rate neglect. Even a strong signal must be combined with how common the event is to begin with.
lessonContent:
Specifics can crowd out generalities.
Strong signals still need the base rate.
Combine both to judge likelihood.
Start with how common the event is.
Share this: add the background frequency to one judgement.

title: Trading Predictions
question: What is a market where people buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events?
correctExplanation: Right. Prices aggregate many traders' beliefs into a running probability estimate.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a prediction market. Money at stake makes participants reveal what they truly believe.
lessonContent:
Prices can aggregate dispersed beliefs.
Stakes encourage honesty.
Markets update as news arrives.
Read prices as probabilities.
Share this: interpret one market or odds figure as a belief.

title: Many Forecasts Together
question: What method improves accuracy by combining the independent forecasts of many people?
correctExplanation: Right. Averaging diverse estimates cancels individual errors and usually beats any single guess.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is ensemble forecasting. Diversity matters, because similar forecasts share the same blind spots.
lessonContent:
Combining estimates cancels random error.
Diversity reduces shared blind spots.
Averages often beat individual experts.
Keep forecasts independent.
Share this: ask three people for an estimate and average them.

title: Many Minds
question: What phenomenon describes a crowd of independent guessers averaging close to the truth?
correctExplanation: Right. Independent errors cancel when many unbiased guesses are pooled, even if few individuals are accurate.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the wisdom of crowds. Independence is essential, since copying others destroys the effect.
lessonContent:
Aggregation can beat expertise.
Independence keeps errors uncorrelated.
Copying neighbours ruins the advantage.
Pool diverse guesses.
Share this: gather several independent guesses before deciding.

title: Thinking Ahead Twice
question: What is the practice of asking not only what will happen but what that outcome will cause next?
correctExplanation: Right. Following the consequences of consequences reveals effects that first-order analysis misses.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is second-order thinking. Decisions that look good immediately can fail once reactions are considered.
lessonContent:
First effects are rarely the last.
Ask what happens after the outcome.
Consider how others respond.
Plan for the consequences of consequences.
Share this: trace one decision two steps past its first result.
